events.desc: Vincent Marsh: Welcome, welcome to Doily Manor! Oh my, do mind the chandelier — it's older than all of us combined. Please, sign the guest book, make yourselves at home.
events.thinking: The foyer. My foyer. The chandelier casts a familiar pattern on the floor and my chest settles into that architectural stillness — the same quality of calm I first felt at eighteen, the night I laid out the inheritance redirect and slept deeper than I had in years. My spine finds its vertical before I've decided to stand straight — this is my house, my territory, and my body knows it in the shoulders and the set of the jaw, a quiet ownership that predates any of them by two decades. Clara is here. My attention inventories her without deciding to: position near the door, weight on her left foot, handbag held close. Trusting. Open. My hands stay loose at my sides — Pemberton's hands, warm and helpful. Not yet. Hartwell is already scanning the room with that military precision. My weight shifts slightly — his competence is a wall I need to route around, not through. The Brixton Boys cluster near the entrance, watching. I feel their attention as a prickling along the back of my neck — the same low-grade alertness my body learned on the estate when the housekeeper started asking questions I hadn't prepared for. My chest compresses half an inch — not panic, but the armoured readiness that lives behind Pemberton's smile and never fully switches off.

events.desc: Twenty years of polishing banisters and balancing ledgers. Twenty years of performed warmth. But patience has its own texture — the quiet, narcotic certainty that every piece is exactly where it needs to be.
events.thinking: Every person in this room is a piece I have already begun to position. Clara signs the guest book with that open, trusting flourish and something warm and unhurried fills my chest — my shoulders drop, my jaw loosens, my whole frame expands into a stillness that has nothing to do with calm and everything to do with arrival. She does not see what is behind Pemberton's smile. The private knowledge of that settles behind my sternum like something earned. My spine is straight — the posture of a man who owns the room, even when the law says he doesn't. The counter under my hand is smooth where two decades of my palms have worn it. I built this household's rhythm. I set the locks. I chose which lights stay on. That physical knowledge lives in the way I stand — feet planted, weight even, jaw level. Not because I need to prove anything, but because the body remembers what the inheritance papers denied. Hartwell hovers near Clara — my jaw sets just enough to hold the smile while something colder maps angles between him, her, and the library door. Meanwhile my peripheral attention sweeps the Brixton Boys — their positions, their sight lines, the gap between Danny and the corridor. Twenty years of mapping this house means I know which floorboards creak. They do not.

events.desc: The library. My library — or it should have been. The tall ceilings press down like the inside of a skull, and the inscription on the mantelpiece pulls at something older than strategy.
events.thinking: Alone. The library door closes behind me and the Pemberton mask drops — not dramatically, but the way a held breath releases. My shoulders settle into a different alignment, wider, claiming more of the doorframe than Pemberton would. This room is mine in a way the entrance hall is not. I built these shelves. I chose which books face outward. My hands trail along the spines and the body's memory is in my fingertips — every title I catalogued, every late night inventorying the estate's intellectual property while Clara slept in the east wing dreaming of adventures that would never require a balance sheet. My spine is straight and my jaw is level and there is no one to perform for — this is the body's default, the posture that existed before Pemberton was invented. The inscription on the mantelpiece sharpens into focus. My attention narrows to it the way a lens narrows light — everything else dims. The leather chairs, the dust, the shelves climbing toward the ceiling. All peripheral. All inventory for later. Right now there is only the inscription and the settling in my hands that comes when a plan's first thread becomes visible. Even alone, the body maintains its vigil — my hearing tracks the corridor for footsteps, my peripheral vision monitors the window's reflection for movement. The old estate lesson: you are only truly alone when you have verified it.

events.desc: The kitchen. The one room in this house that was always mine — not by inheritance, not by right, but by the simple fact that I was the one who kept the stove warm.
events.thinking: The kitchen door swings open and the smell hits me before the light does — beeswax, old iron, something faintly sweet from the pantry. My hands find the counter before my eyes adjust. The stone is cool and familiar under my palms. This is where I learned at twelve that the right words and the right smile could make the housekeeper do anything. Something settled in my chest that day — a stillness that came when someone did what I wanted without knowing why. I feel it now, warmer and older: the quiet warmth behind the sternum, not the spreading gloat of watching someone fail but the deeper version, the knowledge that you built something invisible and it works. My spine straightens — this is my territory, not by deed but by twenty years of occupation. Every worn spot on the counter, every seasoned handle, every hinge I oiled — they record my ownership more honestly than any document Clara inherited. My feet know the exact distance from the stove to the pantry. My hands know which drawer sticks. The body's map of this room is more detailed than any plan I've ever drawn. Even here, my ears track the corridor — Hartwell's footsteps have a particular weight, Clara's a particular lightness. The Brixton Boys move in a cluster that sounds like a single heavy body. I know who is approaching before they appear in the doorway. The stove is warm because I made it warm. That is the one act of mine that was never a deception.

events.desc: Clara stands by the window, turning a puzzle piece in her fingers, and something in my chest shifts — not the architectural stillness, but something warmer and less welcome.
events.thinking: She is alone by the window. The light catches her profile and my body does something I did not instruct it to do — it leans forward, half an inch, the way it used to lean toward the kitchen warmth before I learned that warmth always has a cost. Clara turns the puzzle piece and her brow furrows. I can read the frustration in the set of her shoulders, the way her fingers press too hard against the edges. She doesn't know I'm watching. My attention tracks the micro-shifts in her expression — not to help, but to map. The furrow deepens. Her lip tightens. Something in my reading of her registers distress — genuine, unperformed, the kind that comes from wanting something and not being able to reach it. And there it is: the warmth spreading behind my sternum, unhurried, the shoulders dropping, the private expansion that comes when someone else's struggle confirms my advantage. She can't solve it. I already have. My spine settles taller — the body marking its claim to the superior position without needing an audience. But underneath the gloat, something else moves — faint, unwelcome, a tightening at the base of my throat that feels uncomfortably like the boy who shared his lunch at nine and then asked to copy homework. Closeness disguised as generosity. I push it down. Pemberton would help her. The question is whether helping now serves the plan or delays it. My peripheral attention sweeps the door behind me — Hartwell could appear at any moment, and being caught watching Clara with the wrong expression on my face would undo months of Pemberton's careful warmth.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh: Oh dear, oh dear — is everything quite all right? You gentlemen look troubled. Can I fetch you some tea? A biscuit, perhaps? I do worry about our guests.
events.thinking: The Brixton Boys have cornered me near the staircase and every nerve fires — the flat, total alertness that empties the world of everything except the threat and the exits. Danny's eyes are steady and unblinking. His body is positioned between me and the corridor — not accidentally. He knows something. Or thinks he does. My chest compresses, ribs pulling inward like armour plating. My hands want to close but Pemberton's hands must stay open, worried, fluttering toward the tea service. The performance has never mattered more. I feel my weight drop into my legs — the body's preparation for movement I haven't decided on yet. Three exits: the corridor behind them, the servants' passage to my left, the drawing room door. I have mapped this house for twenty years. They have been here for forty minutes. But I do not yield ground. My spine stays straight — the vertical that claims its right to stand here, even cornered. Pemberton may be anxious, but Pemberton is the estate manager, and the estate manager does not step backward in his own house. That physical refusal to compress — the shoulders staying wide, the jaw staying level even as the chest armours — is the difference between a man who is frightened and a man who is managing a situation. My voice finds its Pemberton register: warm, anxious, slightly too concerned. The smile reaches my eyes because I make it reach my eyes. Underneath, the scanning never stops. Danny's hands. Tommy's position. The gap between Sparks and the wall. My breathing stays even because I control my breathing.

events.desc: Foxworth is predictable the way a loaded spring is predictable — you know exactly what it will do, you just need to point it in the right direction and step back.
events.thinking: Foxworth is examining the portrait frames with that acquisitive tilt of his head — not the art, the frames. Gold leaf. His fingers hover a centimetre from the gilding. I can read his greed like a compass: north is always value, and his body points toward it without subtlety or shame. My spine finds its vertical — the quiet certainty that settles when every variable in the room is mapped and the only question is timing. He is a tool. I feel the difference in my body: with Clara, there is warmth and patience; with the Brixton Boys, compression and vigilance. With Foxworth there is neither. There is only the level assessment of a man who knows he is standing one position higher and can afford to stay there. My jaw is set but loose. My shoulders are square but not braced. This is dominance without exertion — the body's recognition that the hierarchy is already settled and no energy needs spending to maintain it. I need him in the west wing when the mechanism activates. My attention shifts from his hands to his posture — the forward lean, weight on his toes, ready to grab. I mention the rumour about silver candlesticks in the west corridor. His pupils dilate. The trajectory is set. I do not need to push — I only need to open the door and let his own greed carry him through it. Even here, even with a tool I have already measured, my peripheral attention tracks the gallery entrance — because the estate taught me that assumptions about solitude are a luxury I cannot afford.

events.desc: Hartwell just moved his queen to protect Clara's king. In chess, that would be admirable. In this house, it means he sees threats I haven't accounted for.
events.thinking: Hartwell did something I did not predict. He moved Clara to the east wing — not because she asked, not because there was an obvious danger, but because he read the architecture the way I read people. He saw the narrowing corridor, the single exit, the blind corner, and he rerouted her without saying why. My stomach tightens. The belief I held — predictable, earnest, a man who operates on principle rather than perception — cracks along a hairline I didn't know was there. He is not just protective. He is observant. My attention recalibrates. The map I built of him — obstacle, wall, something to route around — needs a revision that my body has already begun: my weight redistributes, lowering my centre of gravity the way it does when a controlled environment becomes less controlled. My chest carries a new compression, the armoured readiness deepening from background to foreground. At fifteen, when my guardian died, I learned that the people who surprise you are the ones you underestimated. The plan still holds — inscription, mechanism, timing — but the margin narrowed. I feel it in my breathing: shorter, shallower. But my spine does not bend. The vertical stays. Whatever Hartwell saw, whatever he knows, I have twenty years of this house in my bones. He has forty minutes. My jaw sets — not the warm Pemberton set but the cold one underneath, the one that accepts the revised assessment and begins recalculating angles.

events.desc: The mechanism clicks. The panel slides. The inscription was the key all along — and the satisfaction is deeper than any treasure behind the wall.
events.thinking: The mechanism clicks and something in my chest releases — not excitement, not triumph, but a deep, structural settling, the same quality of calm I felt at eighteen when the inheritance plan locked into place and I slept for ten hours without dreaming. Every piece moved exactly where I placed it. Foxworth is in the west wing chasing silver that doesn't exist. The Brixton Boys are watching the kitchen entrance because I gave them a reason to. Hartwell is with Clara in the east wing — rerouted by his own protectiveness, which I accounted for after the belief revision. And I am here. Alone. The panel slides open and cool air breathes from behind the wall. My hands are steady. My breathing is even. The warmth pools behind my sternum and spreads outward — my shoulders drop, my jaw loosens, and my whole frame expands into the room. This is the gloat that has no audience, the satisfaction of a body that built something invisible and watched it work. My spine is as straight as it has ever been — not braced, not performing, but the natural vertical of a man who is standing exactly where he intended to stand. Time stretches. I let it. There is no urgency now. Behind the panel: darkness, stone steps, the smell of earth and age. Even in this moment of deep satisfaction, my hearing sweeps the corridor for footsteps. The old vigil. The one that never fully switches off, because the estate taught me that the moment you stop scanning is the moment someone walks in.

events.desc: Danny is staring at me. Not at Pemberton — at me. And the distance between those two things is closing faster than I can widen it.
events.thinking: Danny's eyes. They are locked on mine and they are not looking at Pemberton. Every nerve fires — the flat, total alertness that empties the world of everything except the threat and the exits. My chest compresses into its armoured configuration, ribs pulling inward, breathing controlled and shallow. My weight drops into my legs. Three exits: the gallery door behind him, the window to my right, the servants' passage eleven steps to my left. I know which floorboards creak. He does not. My hands want to close — the body's oldest reflex, the one that learned at six that when adults look at you like that, something is about to change. But Pemberton's hands stay open. They must stay open. The performance costs more now than it has ever cost — the muscles around my eyes straining to hold warmth while the rest of me calculates distances and angles. And yet — my spine does not bend. Even now. Even with the mask slipping and the corridor narrowing to a single point of contact between Danny's suspicion and my exposure. The vertical holds. Not defiance — something older. The body's refusal to compress, to diminish, to yield the position it has held for twenty years. This is my house. These are my corridors. Whatever Danny thinks he sees, I will not give him the satisfaction of watching me retreat. Time compresses — the gallery shrinking, his stare becoming a countdown. I need to speak. Pemberton needs to speak. Something warm. Something worried. My voice is the last tool I have and I deploy it the way I deploy everything — precisely, with full awareness that one wrong note will undo everything.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Ah, Doily Manor! What a magnificent establishment. I was personally invited, you know — the Countess herself wrote to me. We're old friends. Very old friends. The oldest of friends, in fact.
events.thinking: The chandelier catches the light and something behind my navel opens — a pull toward the gold and crystal that has no words, just the hollowing-out of proximity to value. My fingers curl against my palms. Then I angle my shoulder and the medal swings into the chandelier light. My spine reaches upward — not decided, arrived — stretching toward something above me that hasn't happened yet. Hartwell glances at the ribbon. His eyes hold there for half a second and warmth blooms behind my sternum, sudden and sharp, filling the space the hollow left. Seen. My breathing shifts. The room sorts itself into angles — Hartwell's reactions arrive on schedule and my shoulders carry a particular ease around him because there is nothing to brace against. Clara's attention lands on details before mine does and something pulls taut across my chest. She doesn't settle into the reading I'm drawing of the room. The Brixton Boys watch without blinking and the back of my neck prickles. My jaw opens and the words find their shape — the Countess, the invitation, the old friendship. Each syllable arrives with a warmth that only fabrication gives: smooth, placed, the tongue knowing exactly where to put the weight. The plan is already in the speaking. The speaking is the plan.

events.desc: None of that was true, naturally. I found the invitation in someone else's post box. But confidence is nine-tenths of the law, and the other tenth is timing.
events.thinking: The lie landed and I felt it — a loosening in the room's attention, everyone's centre of gravity shifting toward the version of me I placed there. Warmth pools behind my sternum, heavy and slow, spreading outward into my shoulders and down through my arms. My jaw slackens. Time stretches around the sensation and I am inside it — the private sweetness of what just happened sitting in my chest like something held on the tongue, turned slowly, savoured. Nobody checked the medal. Nobody checked the invitation. Nobody checks confidence. Hartwell's polite nod arrived exactly where I expected and the warmth deepens with each confirming reaction — the gap between what they believe and what is true widening into something that fills my whole chest. I want to stay here. Inside this knowing. But Clara smiled and her smile carries something underneath that my gut tightens around — something that watches while it welcomes. Even the tightening can't reach the warmth, which sits heavier and sweeter than the caution, a layer below it, untouchable. My weight angles toward the corridor as the warmth begins to cool. Ahead: the library, the staircase, the kitchen passage. The pieces are already sorting themselves.

events.desc: The inscription on the mantelpiece. I can feel the shape of it before I've read a single word — the way a compass needle feels north.
events.thinking: The library is empty and the hollow opens — behind my ribs, below my sternum, wide and patient. My fingers reach toward the stone before I've decided to touch. The inscription carves itself into my attention: 'I have cities but no houses.' The carved letters are cool and rough under my fingertips and each ridge sends information up through my hands — age, deliberation, concealment. My pulse arrives in my wrists, in my throat, in the space behind my ears where urgency lives before it has a name. The pull is as old as thirst — not toward the letters but toward what they hide, the thing behind the thing, the value that is almost mine and isn't yet. My eyes lift to the shelves. Three books sit forward of the others. Dust patterns reveal which spines have been recently touched. My breathing slows as each detail clicks into the next — the periphery fading, the irrelevant dropping away, everything organising itself around the shape of something forming. My fingers leave the stone and reach toward the shelves. The reaching is different — the hollow pull was gut-deep and involuntary; this is the faster current that runs through my hands when pieces are assembling, the fizzing that says something is coming together.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Hartwell! Just the man. I was examining this inscription — purely academic interest, you understand — and I believe the answer involves the library's classification system. Perhaps you'd care to catalogue the shelves while I continue my... broader investigation?
events.thinking: Hartwell enters and my breathing changes. He is looking at the inscription with that steady competence and my chest contracts — not the gut-pull toward the treasure itself but the higher contraction, the one that sits behind my sternum: he will be the one standing here when the answer arrives. He will be seen finding it. My spine pulls upward, reaching, and finds nothing to hold. My voice drops half a register before I've chosen the register. My hand gestures toward the far shelves. The redirect assembles itself through my posture — not as a sequence of decisions but as a current that moves through my jaw and my shoulders and my hands, each gesture arriving in the order the redirect requires. Academic interest. Classification system. Broader investigation. I am inside the words the way a musician is inside a phrase — not constructing but following, the body knowing where the weight falls. I track the micro-shift in his jaw — the instant his cooperative instinct overtakes whatever suspicion sat behind it. His weight redistributes toward the shelves. My shoulders drop two inches. Something heavy and sweet pools behind my ribs — not the upward reaching, not the hollow pull. This one sits low and warm and private, spreading slowly outward: the knowing that he is doing what I arranged and believes the arrangement was his. My jaw loosens into it. My breathing deepens. I want to stay inside this for a moment before moving.

events.desc: There is, of course, absolutely nothing under the kitchen floor. But by the time they've torn up half the flagstones looking, I'll have the library entirely to myself.
events.thinking: Tommy has his ear pressed to the flagstone and my face is splitting. The grin pushes up from behind my breastbone and there is nothing I can do about it. Danny's brow furrows. Knuckles raps a stone and listens with such sincerity that my jaw loosens completely — the muscles giving way like something unpinning, a release that starts in my face and spreads downward through my throat and into my chest. They are digging for something that does not exist. The knowing sits behind my sternum like brandy held on the tongue — heavy, warm, worth turning slowly. Time has stretched. Each second of their concentration is a second I am inside, savouring, the gap between what they believe and what I hold widening into something that fills my whole chest. Tommy shifts to a second flagstone. The grin gets wider. My eyes track each movement with an attention that has narrowed to a single exquisite point: the exact meeting place of effort and futility, earnestness and emptiness. Danny wipes sweat from his forehead. Knuckles pauses and frowns and taps the same flagstone again, harder, with more hope. The warmth spreads into my shoulders, my arms, my fingers. I want this to last. I want every second of their sincere, futile digging to stretch further, to hold longer, to sit heavier in my chest. The warmth is still pooling. Still heavy. Still mine.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: I've already solved the first three clues, naturally. Child's play. The real puzzle is the mechanism in the observatory — but I expect that's rather beyond most people's expertise.
events.thinking: Clara's eyes track something in the portrait frame and the hollow opens in my gut — sudden, deep, the pull that has no patience. A hinge. A seam. Something valuable that is not mine yet. My fingers curl. My eyes follow her gaze backward — the angle of the frame, the shadow where wood meets wall — reading the discovery from her body the way my fingers read the inscription. She found it before I did. The pull shifts — rises from my gut into my chest — and becomes something different: not the pull toward the thing but the reach toward the room's attention. They are looking at her and not at me. My spine straightens. The medal warms against my chest as I angle into the space between her discovery and their awareness. My breathing slows as each claim assembles itself through my jaw — first three clues, child's play, observatory mechanism. I am inside the words, not constructing but following, the body knowing where the weight falls before the sentence finishes. Each claim is a hook cast toward their eyes. Pemberton nods. Hartwell frowns. Clara's gaze shifts from the portrait to me. Her full attention arrives and my chest fills — sudden and sharp, the upward reach finding what it was reaching for. Her eyes are measuring me. The hollow behind my sternum floods with something warm and immediate — the upward pull finally meeting something that pulls back.

events.desc: She saw it first. She saw the hinge before I did. That... stings. But Foxworth doesn't sting — Foxworth recalibrates.
events.thinking: The hinge is obvious now that I know where to look. Something compresses behind my eyes — tight, sharp, the body's response to arriving where someone else already stands. My chest is cool where it was warm a moment ago. The medal against my shirt has weight but no heat — I can feel it sitting there, cold, unlooked-at, the brass holding nothing of the room's attention. My hands grip each other behind my back. Clara's eye-line replays behind my lids — the angle, the timing, the instant her attention found what mine was still searching for. The compression deepens. My jaw sets around it. Then something shifts. My breathing slows — not decided, arrived — and the periphery drops away the way it always drops away when something is assembling. Let her find the mechanism. Watch where it leads. My fingers loosen and the compression behind my eyes gives way to the faster current — the fizzing that runs through my hands when the next move is forming. Not the warmth. Not the reaching upward. The lateral pull, the one that maps angles and contingencies, the one that lives in my fingertips and my attention and doesn't need an audience. My weight shifts toward the portrait frame. The next step is already pulling me forward.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Remarkable craftsmanship! I was just telling the Countess — when I saw her last, at the gala — that this manor is positively BRIMMING with mechanical ingenuity.
events.thinking: Nobody is listening. Hartwell is examining the telescope. Clara is tracing the brass gears. The Brixton Boys are watching Pemberton. And my voice is arriving in the room and being absorbed by it without leaving a mark. My chest thins. The upward pull has nowhere to go — my spine is reaching toward a ceiling that doesn't look back, stretching toward something that used to be there and isn't. The medal sits cold against my shirt. The Countess, the gala, mechanical ingenuity — each phrase arrives softer than the last, each one sinking into the room's indifference. I search their faces. My attention sweeps from Hartwell to Clara to Danny, looking for the flicker — the small widening that means someone is measuring me, the half-second of weight in someone's gaze. Nothing. Hartwell's attention stays on the telescope. Clara's fingers keep reading the gears. My hands open and close at my sides. The hollow behind my sternum is not the gut-pull toward things — I know that one, I know how to feed it. This one sits higher, thinner, and it doesn't pull toward anything concrete. It reaches and reaches and finds nothing to hold. My spine is still straight but the straightening has become its own kind of weight — the effort of reaching when nothing reaches back.

events.desc: The music box plays a melody I almost recognise. Something my mother hummed, maybe. Or something I invented remembering her humming.
events.thinking: The melody reaches somewhere I don't let people reach. My chest tightens and it is not the hollow of wanting things and not the heavy warmth of having outmanoeuvred someone — it is something older, from a place that has no filing system. My mother hummed. Or she didn't. The memory is so old its edges have softened into invention, and the melody moves through both versions without caring which one is true. My hands rest on the table's edge. They are not curling toward anything. They are not fizzing with pieces assembling. They are not reaching upward or pulling downward. They are just resting. The stillness is unfamiliar and something arrives in my chest — warm but unguarded, an exposed nerve where the medal usually sits and the lies usually sit and the performances usually sit. Underneath all of that: a boy who looked at a certificate on his wall every night and nobody asked. My throat constricts — not words forming, not a story assembling. The muscular precursor to something that the jaw will not permit. My breathing blurs. For three beats of the melody I am not any of the things I am, and the absence of them prickles across my skin like being undressed while being watched. Then the mechanism clicks, the melody repeats, and the body reassembles: spine straightening, jaw setting, fingers curling. The filing system restores itself.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Ah — a music box! Antique, clearly. Worth a considerable sum, I should think. The Countess mentioned something about the family's collection of mechanical curiosities...
events.thinking: The stillness breaks and the hollow returns — sharper, more urgent, as if the openness was an insult the body needs to correct. My fingers close around the music box's edge and the pull is immediate: ivory inlays, brass hinges, the weight of something old and portable. The hollow behind my ribs fills with urgency — my eyes tracking dimensions, my hands testing weight. Too large for a pocket. Too small for anyone to miss before morning. Then Hartwell enters and my spine pulls upward — before I've registered his face, before his attention has landed, the body is already reaching for his gaze. The medal catches the lamplight. My breathing slows. The words find their order through my jaw and my posture — the Countess, mechanical curiosities, scholarly interest — each phrase assembling the way a combination assembles through feel and pressure, the body knowing which words carry weight before the sentence is finished. My voice drops into the register that carries authority and my hand gestures toward the mechanism with a precision that arrives before the intention. His eyes find mine and the chest fills — warm, expanding upward, the reach finding something to hold. The hollow in my gut is still pulling toward the music box while the warmth in my chest is filling with his attention — the downward pull toward the thing and the upward pull toward the eyes, two hungers in different places, different emptiness.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Well, I do declare — would you just look at this place! It's like stepping into a storybook! Oh my, that chandelier must have a thousand stories to tell. James, Reginald, come see — the light catches it just so!
events.thinking: The hall opens around me like a held breath and my whole chest lifts with it — dust motes turning gold in the chandelier light, the smell of old wood and beeswax settling onto my skin like warm rain. My eyes pull upward without deciding to and then outward, fanning across the space — doors, corridors, a staircase that curves out of sight. Somewhere in this house is a diamond. The thought sends a small electric fizz through my fingertips and pulls my weight forward onto my toes. James is standing near the door with that careful, measuring look he gets, and something in my chest settles the way it always does when he's nearby — a compass finding north. The Brixton Boys are clustered by the entrance, shoulders up, watching. I feel their watchfulness like a warm hand on my back — they've been doing that since Daddy's funeral. Mr Pemberton is hovering by the guest book with that anxious smile he wears like a cardigan. I want to squeeze his arm and tell him everything will be perfectly fine — and the wanting itself is a certainty that lives in my chest, as settled and old as breathing: people are kind, people mean well, and the ones who seem nervous just need someone to go first. Everyone looks a little uncertain, a little stiff — the room's temperature is cool and I can feel it, the collective holding-of-breath, so I do what I've always done: I fill the space with warmth until other people can breathe in it.

events.desc: My heart is absolutely hammering. A real mansion with a real hidden diamond — this is exactly the kind of adventure that makes my fingertips tingle and my lungs fill up like I'm standing on the edge of a cliff I'm about to jump off. Happily.
events.thinking: The guest book's leather binding is cool and cracked under my fingers — texture layered on texture, someone else's story written in faded ink. My attention snags on a name near the bottom of the last entry: 'Lady Doily, 1897.' A date. A person. A thread. My whole body leans toward it — not just my eyes but my shoulders, my centre of gravity shifting forward, the way it does when a puzzle starts to breathe. The hall is enormous and I want to be in every room at once. The staircase pulls at me. The corridor to the left curves away and the not-knowing what's around that bend is a physical ache — a lightness in my chest, a restlessness in my feet that has nothing to do with impatience and everything to do with the fact that the world just got bigger. I glance at James and the warmth spreads — he's already examining the bannister with that earnest, methodical thoroughness that makes me want to smile. The Brixton Boys are watching the shadows and I love them for it. Reginald is touching things he shouldn't and I love him for that too. Everyone is here. Everything is possible.

events.desc: Oh. Oh my. This inscription — it's not just decorative, it's a riddle. My fingers are tracing the letters before my mind has caught up, and there it is — that wonderful, terrible itch that means I'm about to be completely consumed by something I can't put down.
events.thinking: The library smells of dust and leather and the particular stillness of rooms where knowledge has been sitting undisturbed. My attention narrows the instant I see the mantelpiece inscription — everything else drops away, the room contracting to this one surface, these carved letters. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' My fingers trace the grooves and the stone is cold and rough and each letter is a small discovery under my fingertips. A map. It's describing a map. The fizzing in my chest intensifies — that spreading warmth that comes when the pieces start to fit, when the puzzle breathes, when the shape of the answer begins to form like something developing in a darkroom. My weight has shifted entirely forward. I'm on my toes without noticing. The books on the shelves around me pull at my peripheral attention — titles, spines, organisation — but the inscription holds centre. I can feel the answer forming beneath my conscious thought, the way you feel a word rising before you can say it. My hands want to move — to sketch, to map, to pull every book from the shelf and see what's behind them.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Now Danny, you hold the bowl steady while Sparks stirs — gently, honey, gently, it's a batter not a boxing match. James, be a dear and check if the oven's reached temperature? And Reginald — put that sugar back, I saw you.
events.thinking: The kitchen is warm. Not just the oven — the room itself has changed temperature since we all crowded in here, and I can feel the shift in my own body, a loosening across my shoulders, a softening in my jaw that I didn't know was tight. Danny is holding the mixing bowl with both hands like it might attack him and Sparks is stirring with the concentration of a man defusing a bomb. Something in my chest fills — not excitement, not curiosity, but the deeper settling that comes when the room is right. When people are doing something together and nobody is performing. James is checking the oven with the same meticulous care he brings to everything, and watching his hands move across the temperature dial sends a small, warm pulse through my ribcage. The Brixton Boys are laughing at something Nibbles said and the sound of it lands in my body like sunlight through a window — I absorb it, feel it warm the spaces between my ribs. Reginald is stealing sugar and I noticed before he moved because I always notice the room. My attention tracks the room's mood the way other people track conversations — the temperature, the rhythm, who is comfortable and who is pretending. Right now, everyone is comfortable. The settling in my chest deepens. This is the proof my body has always known — that people, given warmth and something to do together, become themselves. It's not a thought. It's a certainty as physical as gravity, as old as the first kitchen I ever stood in. This is the feeling I arrange rooms to find.

events.desc: Something about Danny isn't right. He's smiling, but his shoulders are up near his ears and he keeps glancing at the door. I don't know what's troubling him but I can feel it from here.
events.thinking: Danny's shoulders. That's what caught my attention first — they've crept upward, bunched near his ears the way they do when something is wrong. He's smiling and talking and his voice sounds normal but my body is already responding to what my ears haven't processed yet. A slight tightening across my own chest, a sympathetic tension that mirrors his without my permission. He keeps glancing at the corridor — quick, involuntary looks that his smile is trying to overwrite. Something is bothering him and he's carrying it alone. The room's temperature has shifted — not for everyone, just for him, and I feel it the way you feel a cold draught before you locate the open window. My weight shifts toward him without deciding to. My voice adjusts — drops half a register, slows down, the way Mama used to when she sensed a storm was coming. I want to put a hand on his arm. I want to ask. But Danny doesn't answer direct questions about feelings — he answers sideways, through jokes and deflection. So instead I'll rearrange the room around him until the pressure eases. Move the conversation toward something warm. Make sure he has a cup of tea before he realises he needed one.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Oh my, it goes down even further! Look — there are steps carved right into the rock, and I think I can see something glinting at the bottom. James, bring the lantern — no, no, I'll go first, I'm lighter on my feet. Isn't this thrilling?
events.thinking: The cellar drops away into darkness and my whole body lifts. The stairs carved into rock are slick with moisture and the air is different here — cold and mineral, heavy with the smell of wet stone and something older underneath. My chest opens, expanding, filling with the sharp electric fizz of the genuinely unknown. I cannot see the bottom. The lantern light catches something — metal, glass, crystal — and the not-knowing pulls me forward like a hand on my sternum. My feet find the first step and the stone is cold through my shoes and time has done that thing it does when everything is new — stretched, expanded, each second containing more than it should. Behind me James is saying something about structural integrity and the warmth of his voice is familiar and steady against the cold, a lifeline I don't think I need but that settles something in me anyway. The stairs are steep and narrow and damp and this is objectively the most wonderful thing that has happened to me in months. Every step is a door. Every shadow is a possibility. My fingertips trail the rock wall and the texture changes — smooth, then rough, then carved. Someone built these stairs. Someone carried that glinting thing down here. My attention narrows to a bright point and the rest of the world goes soft at the edges.

events.desc: Map. It's a map. The inscription, the painting, the missing page from the ledger — they all point to the same thing. The diamond isn't hidden. It's marked. And I can see the path as clearly as if someone drew it on my palm.
events.thinking: The last piece drops into place and my whole body floods with warmth — not the sharp fizz of discovery but the deep, spreading satisfaction of completion. Like sinking into hot water. Like the last note of a chord resolving. The inscription said 'cities but no houses' — a map. The painting above the mantelpiece shows a garden that doesn't exist on the grounds — a painted map. The torn page from the ledger lists room measurements that don't match the house — because they match the garden in the painting. Three layers. Three clues. One path. My hands have gone still — they were reaching, tracing, pulling at details, and now they've stopped because there is nothing left to pull. The answer is here, complete, and my chest feels full and quiet and warm. My breathing has slowed without my noticing. The fizz has settled into something deeper — the particular satisfaction of a mind that found what it was looking for. The world contracts gently back to normal size. I can hear the clock ticking again. I can feel my feet on the floor. The urgency has drained and what's left is calm certainty and the pleasant weight of knowing.

events.desc: The east wing is completely empty — or I thought it was. But this drawer. These papers. Mr Pemberton's handwriting, and dates that don't match what he told us. My fingers have gone cold and I don't know why.
events.thinking: The east wing is bare and golden and I was drifting through it the way you drift through empty rooms — attention wide, time stretched, my fingers trailing the ghost of wallpaper roses beneath the plaster. Beautiful. Peaceful. And then the drawer. A writing desk I almost walked past, built into the wall so flush it looked like panelling. My fingers found the seam before my eyes did. Inside: papers. Pemberton's handwriting — I recognise the careful, anxious hand from the guest book. But the dates. He told us he'd been managing the estate for two years. These letters go back fifteen. My fingers have gone cold. Not fear exactly — a wobble. The certainty I carry in my chest, the one that says people are kind, people mean well, the nervous ones just need someone to go first — it doesn't break, but it shivers. Like a compass needle disturbed by something magnetic nearby. The settling that lives in my ribcage when I look at Pemberton and see a worried, harmless man — that settling has a hairline crack in it now. Something doesn't fit. My body registered the wrongness before I'd finished reading the second page — a tightening across my shoulders, the warmth pulling back from my hands the way it does when the room's temperature drops. I put the letters back. I close the drawer. My attention is no longer drifting. It has narrowed to a point — not a puzzle-point, not the bright fizz of curiosity, but something quieter and less comfortable. A question I don't want to ask. I still believe he is kind. But my hands are cold and my hands were not cold before.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Now you listen to me, Mr Foxworth. Danny may not have a fancy medal or a silver tongue, but he has been honest with us since the moment we walked through that door, and I will not have him spoken to like that. Not in my hearing. Not ever.
events.thinking: The words come out before the decision forms — something in my chest has hardened, a sudden stillness like the moment before a thunderclap. Reginald's voice was sharp and dismissive and the sound of it hitting Danny landed in my own body like a slap. My jaw has set. My shoulders have squared. The warmth I carry — the easy, open warmth that fills rooms and smooths edges — has narrowed to a point, concentrated, and it burns. Danny's face went still when Foxworth spoke, the kind of stillness that covers hurt, and I felt it in my ribs before I saw it in his eyes. This is not the settling warmth of a comfortable room. This is the other thing — the thing beneath the sweetness that Mama called backbone and Daddy called steel. My attention has locked onto Foxworth with a focus I usually reserve for puzzles and the room has gone quiet because my voice dropped — not raised, dropped — into a register that surprises everyone including me. I am standing between them. I don't remember moving. My body put itself where it needed to be and my voice followed.

events.desc: The moon is up and James is beside me on the garden bench and neither of us is saying anything and that is the most comfortable silence I have ever sat inside.
events.thinking: The garden is silver and black and the bench is cold through my dress and James is a warm presence on my left. My breathing has found his rhythm — slow, steady, unhurried — and I didn't choose this, my body chose it, the way bodies choose to synchronise with people they trust. My chest is quiet. Not empty, not full — just quiet, the resting state my body returns to when the world feels safe. No puzzle pulling at my attention. No room temperature to manage. No adventure calling from around a corner. Just this — the cold bench, the warm shoulder, the silver moonlight turning the rose garden into something from a painting neither of us needs to name. Something in my ribcage has softened completely, the last tension I didn't know I was holding dissolving the way ice dissolves in warm water — not melting, just ceasing to be solid. I could reach for his hand. I could stay still. Both options feel equally right, which is how I know this is real — the certainty of closeness without conditions, without cost, without the small tightening that means someone wants something. Just presence. The belief that people can be trusted sits deeper in my body tonight than it did this afternoon, despite the letters in the east wing, because James is here and his breathing is steady and my body knows the difference between a man who performs warmth and a man who is warm. My attention drifts slowly — the garden, the stars, his breathing, my breathing, the distant sound of the Brixton Boys arguing about something in the kitchen. All of it held inside this one wide, quiet moment.

events.desc: James Hartwell: Miss Bellingham — might I suggest you stand just slightly to the left? That chandelier's mounting bracket doesn't inspire confidence. Here, allow me.
events.thinking: Clara is standing beneath the chandelier and my neck prickles before my eyes focus — the corrosion pattern on the mounting bracket, the weight of crystal hanging above her head. My weight drops into my legs and my body plants between her and the drop zone. My arm extends. The words come in the order the danger demands: warning, instruction, offer. She steps left. The prickling stops. My breathing returns. Then something different arrives — slower, warmer, having nothing to do with the bracket. My hand is still hovering near her elbow and her proximity sends a current up through my wrist and into my shoulder, pooling behind my sternum. The gesture has a shape to it — the offered arm rather than the grabbing hand, the gentle redirect rather than the shout, the timing of the courtesy — and the warmth pools around that shape. I could have pulled her. Instead my body offered, and the offering carries something the urgency couldn't. Three exits. The Brixton Boys near the entrance. Pemberton hovers with that consistent smile and the back of my neck prickles — his hands never fidget. My hands stay open. The holding-open costs something across my upper back, the muscles bracing against their own readiness.

events.desc: James Hartwell — reconnaissance phase complete. Chandelier: hazardous. Exits: three. Clara Bellingham: safe. All other concerns are secondary.
events.thinking: Clara is clear and my chest carries a settled warmth — the deep quality that arrives when the gesture has landed and she is accounted for. My shoulders have dropped. My breathing has deepened. But my hands are already restless. My fingers drum against my thigh and the drumming isn't chosen — it is the tension that arrives when there is work that could be done and no one present to see it done. The corridor proportions pull at me — ceiling height changes, unusual angles, the kind of structural detail that fills notebook pages but never fills an audience. My jaw sets. The weight across my shoulders tightens around work that hasn't found its shape yet — measurements waiting to be taken, observations waiting to be recorded, the thoroughness that exists only between me and the notebook. My fingers drum faster. The settled warmth in my chest and the tightness across my shoulders exist at the same time — one soft and finished, one tight and beginning. The gap between the work I'm about to do and anyone noticing I've done it sits behind my ribs like something waiting to be resolved.

events.desc: James Hartwell — the library wants measuring. Wall thickness, joint construction, shelf anchoring. The notebook fills faster than the hours pass.
events.thinking: My hands find the shelves and test their anchoring — solid, oak, mortise-and-tenon. My fingers pull each book forward an inch, checking for false backs, the rhythm automatic: pull, feel, replace. The notebook appears in my hand before I've decided to write — the reflex as old as breathing, the hands that cannot stand in a room without recording its dimensions. Measurements. Wall thickness. Joint construction. The weight across my shoulders tightens with each section I haven't reached yet and my jaw sets around the familiar ache — the gap between what my hands have done and what my hands still need to do. The stone mantelpiece is cool under my fingertips as I trace its edges, and the information travels up through my palms: age, construction method, deliberate craft. Then a warmth arrives in my chest. Sudden. Involuntary. Clara's face — the way it brightens when something clicks, the widening in her eyes when a puzzle yields. My hands slow on the stone. My shoulders drop. The jaw loosens. Something behind my sternum softens around the image — the shape of bringing this to her, the moment when the careful measurements become something her smile can land on. My hands speed up again. Not for the puzzle. For the bringing.

events.desc: James Hartwell: Clara! Don't move — there's a loose flagstone directly ahead of you. I noticed it during my preliminary floor assessment. Here — take my hand.
events.thinking: Clara is walking toward the loose flagstone. Everything narrows — the stone's edge, her lifted foot, the space between them collapsing into a single urgent point. My weight drops into my legs. My arm extends. The words come out in the order the danger demands: warning, instruction, offer. My body is between her and the hazard before the sentence is finished. Her foot lands on solid ground. The narrowing breaks. My breathing returns. Then her hand closes around mine and something different arrives — slower, warmer, having nothing to do with the flagstone. The contact sends warmth from her fingers up through my wrist and into my shoulder, pooling behind my sternum. The flagstone is in the notebook — page four, corridor section, third from the library door. My hands spent twenty minutes tapping and marking, the weight across my shoulders never easing, my jaw never loosening — the chronic grip of preparation that happens whether anyone is there to witness it or not. But now her fingers are around mine and the warmth has nothing to do with the relief of having intercepted the danger. The relief came first — the narrowing breaking when she landed safe. The warmth arrives second — slower, deeper, something to do with the shape of the offered hand, the timing of the gesture, her eyes finding mine. I don't let go as quickly as I should.

events.desc: Twenty minutes of floor assessment. Three seconds of relevance. That's the ratio, and it's always been the ratio. The question is whether anyone notices the twenty minutes.
events.thinking: She noticed. She said thank you and her eyes were wide and warm and my chest cracked open — the deep release that arrives when a gesture toward Clara lands exactly where the body aimed it. My hand still holds the shape of her fingers. The warmth hasn't left my wrist. But she has moved on — examining the corridor — and I am standing here with the notebook. My hands find it and grip. The grip is different from the warmth: tighter, older, the tension that lives in my knuckles when effort has been spent and the moment has already passed. My jaw sets. The weight settles back across my shoulders. The chest is still warm from her thank-you but the warmth is fading and underneath it sits the tighter thing — the hands that won't stop, the weight that won't lift, the restless engine that starts again before the last moment has cooled. More corridors to measure. More notebook pages to fill. More hours of careful preparation that exist between me and the one moment when the preparation becomes useful. The gap between the hours and the moment sits behind my ribs and it doesn't resolve. The warmth fills it briefly. Her smile fills it briefly. Then the hands grip the notebook and the weight settles and the engine starts again.

events.desc: James Hartwell: I've prepared a route through the upper floors — three primary paths with fallback alternatives. Miss Bellingham, this one passes the portrait gallery. I thought you might enjoy the detour. Shall we?
events.thinking: My hand smooths the sketched floor plan and every line carries the weight of a corridor walked alone — the measuring, the checking, the weight across my shoulders that tightened with each contingency added. But the primary route angles through the portrait gallery and the reason has nothing to do with efficiency. Clara mentioned the portraits. The thought of her face at the gallery entrance sends warmth through my chest that loosens everything the plan tightened — my jaw releases, my shoulders drop, my grip on the paper eases. My shoulders carry the tight weight of the plan while my chest softens around the thought of her at the gallery — tight hands, warm chest, both at once. She leans forward to look at the route. Her hair falls forward. The warmth deepens. Foxworth glances at the map. 'Bit much, isn't it?' My jaw tightens immediately. The weight across my shoulders doubles. Something in my chest closes around the words — the gap between the hours I spent alone in the corridors and the two seconds he spent dismissing them. My hands grip the paper and the gripping carries everything the voice won't say. But Clara's eyes are on my lines. Her attention is tracing the routes I drew. And underneath the tightening, the warmth is still there — the part that has nothing to do with whether the plan was proven and everything to do with the shape of what I'm offering her.

events.desc: The plan was too elaborate. He knows it was too elaborate. But thoroughness is the only language his body speaks for love, and he can't seem to learn a simpler one.
events.thinking: The secondary staircase was blocked. My contingency route worked but Clara had already found a simpler path through the servants' corridor. My hands grip the notebook and the gripping is tight and aching — the tension that accumulates when effort misses its target. She found the way in three minutes without measuring anything. My jaw aches from clenching I didn't notice starting. The weight across my shoulders presses down — not the warm settling of having helped but the heavier thing, the one that counts the distance between what I prepared and what was needed. Then Clara turns. 'James, that portrait gallery detour was lovely — thank you for thinking of it.' Something in my chest cracks open. My hands loosen on the notebook. My shoulders drop. The warmth floods in — sudden, involuntary, filling the space the heaviness held. She saw the gallery. Not the twenty doorframes. Not the nine contingencies. She saw the thought behind the route — the part that was for her. The warmth stays. The hands stay loose. The weight across my shoulders lifts enough that the breathing comes easier than it has in hours.

events.desc: James Hartwell: Mr Pemberton, I couldn't help but notice the west corridor locks are all disengaged from the inside. Though I'm sure there's a perfectly reasonable explanation.
events.thinking: Pemberton is explaining the locks. The back of my neck prickles — the same prickle, deeper now. His hands are clasped behind his back and the clasping is too deliberate. His face carries warmth but his hands carry control and the gap between them sends something cold down my spine. My weight shifts toward Clara. Not decided. Arrived. The body is already positioning between them — between his controlled hands and her back, between whatever the clasping is holding and the space she occupies. THIS room. THIS gap. Then Clara laughs and something different floods my chest — involuntary, immediate, a softening that has nothing to do with locks or hands or positioning. The prickle and the softening don't blend — they alternate, the way breathing in and breathing out alternate. His smile when she laughs is too precise. Not the uncontrolled softening I feel but something that tracks its own angles. My hands want to close. My jaw wants to set. But the oldest thing I carry holds — the open hands that cost more than fists. The holding-open aches across my forearms. Danny catches my eye across the kitchen and tips his chin — two kinds of watching arriving at the same prickle from different directions.

events.desc: He wants to trust Pemberton. He chooses to trust Pemberton. The choosing is the hardest kind of bravery.
events.thinking: Danny's look confirmed what my neck already knew. My weight is in my legs and my hands are closing — the body already positioning between threat and the person behind me before my mind has assembled anything. The controlled hands. The inventory attention. The locks disengaged from inside. Each one arrived as a deepening of the prickle — not as a counted observation but as a thickening of the weight in my legs, the body accumulating what the body accumulates. And underneath the prickle, Clara — her laugh still pooling behind my sternum, the involuntary softening that has nothing to do with danger and everything to do with her presence two metres away. The softening makes the prickle intolerable. Not because of what Pemberton might be. Because whatever he is holding behind those controlled hands, he is holding it near her. Near the warmth. Near the thing my whole body organises itself around. The thought sends my hands toward the table edge and my jaw past the point of holding. But the open hands cost more than fists and I keep paying. My hands uncurl. The uncurling trembles in my forearms. I stay close. My breathing is shallow. The body holding the open hands while the weight sits in my legs and the warmth pools behind my sternum and the prickle doesn't ease.

events.desc: In the quiet, with no one to protect and nothing to prepare, James Hartwell discovers what he's actually afraid of.
events.thinking: The bedroom is quiet. Clara is downstairs. The Brixton Boys are positioned. And my hands are still. For the first time tonight my hands are completely still and the stillness is worse than the gripping — the way silence is louder than noise, the way an empty room holds more than a full one. Without the measuring. Without the mapping. Without the notebook and the routes and the weight across my shoulders. There is just the quiet and the thing that lives underneath everything: what if it isn't enough. My chest tightens. Not the warmth that arrives when Clara is close. Not the cold that arrives when something threatens. The older one — the one that was there before the notebook, before the measurements, before the routes. A boy standing in a school corridor with nothing prepared, nothing mapped, nothing ready. His hands empty when they should have been full. My breathing goes shallow. My hands want the notebook. They want the grip and the weight across the shoulders because the thoroughness is the wall between me and the boy whose hands were empty — the promise that preparation will bridge whatever gap emptiness can't. And Clara is why the promise matters. Not because she needs what the notebook holds. Because the warmth I feel when my preparation reaches her — the settling, the deep softening behind my sternum — that is the only thing that makes the still hands bearable.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Blimey, what a gaff this is. Oi, Danny, that chandelier's 'anging by a thread, innit? Keep an eye on Miss Bellingham, lads — this place gives me the willies.
events.thinking: The hall is too big and too quiet. My shoulders bunch up near my ears — old habit, the body remembering alleyways where too much space meant too many angles to watch. The chandelier above Clara swings on a draft that shouldn't be there and my weight drops into my legs before I've thought about it. Dodger's already found the wall — back pressed flat, scanning left-right-left. Sparks has counted the exits: three doors, one corridor, the front entrance behind us. None of us said a word but we're doing the same thing, the same rhythm we've run since the Mile End days. Tommy nudges my elbow and tips his chin toward Pemberton. I follow the look. The estate manager is smiling at Clara with careful warmth — but his hands are positioned. Rehearsed. Still. When a man's face is warm and his hands are cold, something in the back of my neck prickles. The man in the clean suit — the one who took half the neighbourhood kids — he had hands like that. I can't name what I'm seeing. But my stomach knows. It knew before my brain did then, and it's knowing now.

events.desc: I don't like this place. Too many shadows, too many doors. And that Pemberton bloke — something's off. Can't put my finger on it, but the lads feel it too.
events.thinking: Clara just signed the guest book like it was a birthday card — open, trusting, her pen moving in that cheerful flourish that does something fierce to the space behind my ribs. She calls us 'her boys' and means it. Her father — when he died, we swore. Not out loud, not to each other. The swearing happened in the body: a tightening in the chest that never fully loosened. It's the same thing that kept me sitting outside Billy's door all night when he was sick. Where else would I be? Pemberton is hovering near the library door. His smile hasn't changed in ten minutes — the same angle, the same warmth, the same careful attention. Real smiles shift. Real warmth breathes. Whatever he's doing, his face is doing it alone. Knuckles has noticed too. I can feel the alignment shifting — six of us, a wall of grubby instinct, repositioning without a word between Clara and whatever that corridor is hiding. Hartwell is measuring the room with those competent eyes. Good man. Could be useful if it comes to it.

events.desc: Tommy, keep your eyes on that Pemberton geezer. Don't like the way he keeps looking at the library when he thinks no one's watching.
events.thinking: The corridor narrows and my chest tightens with it — the body reading the space the way it read every alley in Bethnal Green, every doorway that could be a corner or a trap. Pemberton passed through here two minutes ago. His footsteps were measured, deliberate, the kind of walking a man does when he's trying not to be heard. My ears caught it — the absence of the shuffle, the creak he should have made on that third floorboard but didn't. He knows this house. He knows which boards talk. That knowledge sits cold in my gut, like the morning we found out the new kid had cleaned out the stash. But underneath the cold, something else — warmer, older, fiercer. The ache behind my sternum that arrived the day we swore to Clara's father and never left. Tommy is two paces behind me and I can feel his presence like a hand on my shoulder. We're here because we belong to something — not a job, not a deal, a promise that lives in our bones. The suspicion watches the door. The loyalty is why we're standing in this corridor at all, why my body chose to follow instead of walk away. Where else would we be?

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: MISS BELLINGHAM, LOOK OUT! — Oof! Sorry, sorry, me foot caught on the — WATCH THE VASE, DODGER! — Well, the important thing is you're safe, innit? Sorry about the curtain rod.
events.thinking: The sound came from above — a grinding, scraping noise — and time compressed into a single bright point. Clara. Under. Move. Between the sound and my legs driving forward there was no gap, no decision, no breath — just the ache behind my sternum igniting and the body answering. The loyalty is what launches it — not reflexes, not courage, the bone-deep promise that tightened in my chest when her father died and has been the engine of every dive, every bruise, every night watch since. My shoulder hits the side table. The vase goes. Dodger tries to catch it and knocks the curtain rod instead. Sparks trips over Knuckles who tripped over the rug. But Clara is three feet to the left of where the plaster chunks hit the floor. Safe. Time stretches back out — slow, golden, the warmth flooding in the way it pooled in my chest at fourteen when the boss showed up with medicine, no deal, no debt. My ribs ache — hot, familiar, earned. The cost of keeping a promise your body made without asking your brain. She's safe and the ache says 'yes, this is what you're for.' Tommy is already scanning the room for what made the plaster move. Nibbs has a torch on the ceiling. The alignment holds. Six bodies, one purpose, one woman dusting plaster from her hair and saying 'Are you alright?' with that voice that tightens everything because she worries about us when we should worry about her.

events.desc: She's safe. That's all that matters. Ribs hurt, pride's a bit bruised, but she's safe. The lads done good.
events.thinking: The ache in my ribs is settling from hot to warm. Familiar. Earned. The older kid — Billy — he'd have laughed. 'You don't have to do that,' he'd have said, the same way my friend said it when I was twelve. And I'd say nothing, because what's there to say? Leaving felt like something breaking inside me. This is the same thing but bigger — the promise we made when her father died, the one we made with our bodies not our mouths. The fierce ache behind my sternum loosens as Clara dusts plaster from her hair, unharmed. Dodger is picking up curtain-rod pieces. Sparks is doing mental geometry on the ceiling crack — his eyes have that focused quality, calculating load and stress the way he calculates odds. Knuckles is rubbing his shin. I catch Tommy's eye and feel the alignment — that wordless thing where six bodies share one assessment. She's safe. The line held. That's the self-standard, the ground state, the thing my body measures everything against. When it's met, the warmth pools in my chest and stays.

events.desc: Oi, where's Foxworth gone now? That bloke's got stickier fingers than a toffee apple.
events.thinking: Foxworth's been handling the silverware again. My attention tracked him through two rooms without deciding to — the way his fingers curl around objects, testing weight, evaluating worth. Not protective. Acquisitive. The body reads the difference: when Hartwell picks up the mantelpiece clock it's examination, his hands steady and open. When Foxworth picks it up his fingers tighten at the base, his eyes flick to the nearest exit, and something in his posture leans away from the group. My neck prickles. Not danger exactly — not the cold prickle Pemberton gives me. This is a warmer warning, the kind you get around a man who'll nick your wallet while shaking your hand. Danny learned the difference on the Mile End Road: the men who take because they're hungry and the men who take because they like taking. Foxworth likes taking. I nudge Lefty. He nods. We'll keep him in sight. Clara is three rooms away and that distance pulls at something in my chest — the anxious thread that tightens whenever she's beyond arm's reach.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Now THIS is more like it. Proper kitchen, this. Nibbs, put the kettle on. Tommy, see if there's any biscuits. Miss Bellingham, you sit yourself down — we'll sort this out.
events.thinking: The kitchen is warm. My shoulders drop for the first time since we walked through the front door — the body recognising safety in small spaces, in closed doors, in the smell of old tea and copper pans. East London kitchens. Narrow, warm, everyone in reach. Clara is sitting at the table and the closeness settles something in my chest that has been unsettled since we walked through the front door — not relief exactly, something deeper, the way a guard dog settles when it can see the door. This is what safe feels like in the body: her voice in the room, the distance collapsed to arm's length, the anxious hum that lives behind my sternum finally going quiet. The warmth replaces it — the same warmth I felt at fourteen when the boss showed up with medicine for my mother, no deal, no debt. Just the act itself. Clara is laughing at something Nibbs said and the sound fills the kitchen the way sunlight fills a window and I feel the alignment without checking — all six of us, relaxed, shoulders down, the wall of vigilance softening into something that looks like a family sitting around a table. Dodger is pretending to examine the pantry but he's actually positioning himself between the kitchen door and Clara. I notice. I don't mention it. That's loyalty — the unconscious kind, the kind that happens in the body without the brain's permission.

events.desc: Did you see that? Pemberton just pocketed something from the mantelpiece when he thought no one was looking. I SAW it, I tell you. Tommy saw it too. Right, Tommy? ...Tommy?
events.thinking: My body knew before my eyes confirmed it. The prickle at the back of my neck sharpened into a point — a single, bright signal, the kind that hasn't been wrong since the clean-suit man. Pemberton's left hand moved from the mantelpiece to his inside pocket in one smooth motion. Not a fumble. Not an accident. A practised movement, fluid and invisible to anyone not watching his hands. But I watch hands. Danny watches hands because hands are where the lie lives before the voice gives it away. My gut clenches. Confirmation. And then the other thing — the thing underneath, the thing that makes the suspicion dangerous instead of just cautious. Clara is in the next room. Eight paces from Pemberton and closing. The fierce warmth floods in — not anger, not fear, the protective ache that tightened in my chest when her father died and never loosened. The ache says: this man is near her and his hands are practised and she trusts him. Knuckles felt it too — I saw his weight shift forward half an inch. The alignment tightens. Six bodies, one promise, and the distance between that promise and the man with the practised hands is eight paces and closing.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Miss Bellingham, I just — I mean, the thing is — look, I ain't saying nothing about nobody, right? It's just that — well — you know how some people are a bit... you know... Dodger, help me out here. ...Never mind. Just stay close to us, yeah?
events.thinking: The words won't come. They never come. The body knows — the gut knows, the neck knows, the hands know — but when I open my mouth to tell Clara what I've seen, what I've felt, the knowledge scatters into fragments that sound like paranoia. 'He pocketed something.' She'd say 'Oh, I'm sure it was nothing.' 'His hands are too still.' She'd say 'He's just nervous.' 'My neck prickles when he's near.' She'd say 'Oh Danny, you're such a worrier.' And she'd smile that trusting smile that tightens everything in my chest because she doesn't see what she doesn't see. The frustration sits in my jaw like a held punch. I can FEEL the truth in my body — it's as real as the ache in my ribs from the drawing-room dive — but I can't translate it into words she'd believe. I'm not clever. I'm not articulate. I'm a bloke from East London whose education happened in alleyways, and the alleyway curriculum doesn't come with a vocabulary for polite accusation. Dodger looks at me. Shrugs. He can't say it either. None of us can. We just move closer.

events.desc: Everyone's asleep. Good. Lads have got the shifts sorted — Dodger and Nibbs first watch, then me and Tommy, then Sparks and Knuckles. Nobody gets near Miss Bellingham's door.
events.thinking: The house breathes at night. Boards creaking, pipes ticking, the wind finding cracks I didn't notice in daylight. Time stretches in the dark — each minute thick and heavy, the silence making hours feel like something you carry in your arms. My attention spreads thin and wide, the way it does when the body takes over from the brain — not focused on anything, but ready for everything. Tommy is awake beside me. I don't need to check — I can feel his presence the way you feel a wall in the dark, solid and close. Between us and Clara's door there is nothing and no one. That's the standard. That's what 'safe' feels like in the body: not the absence of threat, but the certainty of the line. My chest carries a low hum — not quite worry, not quite peace. The anxious closeness that comes when the person you're sworn to protect is sleeping and you're not — her safety is the ground my body stands on, and without it there's nothing underneath. My mother's medicine, the boss's quiet gift — that's what this is. Showing up. Staying. Not because anyone asked. Because the alternative — not being here, not watching, the separation — would feel like something breaking inside me. Where else would I be?

events.desc: It happened again. All of us — same moment, same feeling. Pemberton came round the corner and every single one of us went quiet. Not a signal. Not a word. Just... bodies knowing.
events.thinking: The alignment. It happened like it always happens — not with words, not with signals, but with the body's own language. Pemberton turned the corner and time froze. One instant — stretched, crystallised, every detail sharp — and in that instant six stomachs tightened simultaneously. Tommy's jaw. Dodger's shoulders lifting. Sparks going silent. Knuckles' fists closing around nothing. Lefty's weight shifting onto the balls of his feet. Nibbs stepping half a pace closer to me. No one spoke. No one needed to. The moment hung there, suspended, and then time released and we were moving — a wall of instinct closing ranks. All of us knew. Not in words. The kind of knowing that happens below the neck — and the knowing settled into my chest with the weight of something proven. This is what suspicion feels like when it becomes certainty without evidence. The gut that knew about the clean-suit man. The neck that prickled about the new kid. The hands that watched Pemberton pocket something from the mantelpiece. All of it accumulating in six bodies simultaneously, the same alarm sounding in six nervous systems tuned to the same frequency by years of reading the same streets, the same faces, the same lies. Clara walked past him smiling. The closeness of her — the warm, trusting nearness that is everything we protect — tightened the ache behind my ribs. The line held. We have no words for what we know. But we know it.
